segs.text: Section sixteen. Drug transporters and P glycoprotein. Transporters are the second big area of pharmacogenomics, and P glycoprotein, P G P, is the best characterized. It is an efflux transporter in the gut wall: it pumps drugs out of gut cells back into the inside of the gut, the lumen, which limits how much is absorbed.

Transporters move drugs across the gut, excrete them into bile and urine, and carry them across the blood brain barrier. They sit in gut cells, enterocytes, liver cells, hepatocytes, and kidney proximal tubule cells, on both the luminal side and the blood side, called basolateral. She said, Remember, B is for blood side.

On the plasma and cellular concentration curves, the dashed line is the variant. With low activity P G P, less drug is pumped back into the lumen, so the cellular concentration rises sharply and more reaches the blood, the same effect as a P G P inhibitor. Increased intestinal P G P expression can limit absorption; decreased expression may give plasma concentrations above the therapeutic range.

P G P is coded by A B C B one, also called M D R one, multidrug resistance one: two names, one gene, and A B C B one is the newer. P G P affects the distribution of digoxin, cyclosporine, tacrolimus and the antiretroviral protease inhibitors. Digoxin is her main example because its therapeutic index is narrow: with low activity P G P, a normal dose can push the heart rate far too low, so the dose would be adjusted.

Three common snips sit in exon twelve, C twelve thirty six T, exon twenty one, G twenty six seventy seven T, and exon twenty six, C thirty four thirty five T. Exons twenty one and twenty six are both linked to digoxin. Only exon twenty six is linked to protease inhibitor levels and clinical effects; in the initial studies exon twenty one was not. P G P is still hard to pin down: a variant's effect changes with the drug, lab cell systems disagree, and the partner transporters on the blood side are not all characterized.
